title: After Studying Abroad at the University of Adelaide
paragraphs: I have many reasons for joining this study abroad program, but the most fundamental is nothing other than curiosity, simply because it seemed interesting. Another reason was that, considering the possibility of working overseas in the future, I wanted to test how far I could cope in a different cultural and linguistic sphere.

The place where I was allowed to study abroad this time was the University of Adelaide in Australia, where I did clerkships in the Burn Unit, the Acute Medical Unit and the Orthopedics and trauma unit.

First, in the Burn Unit, I observed burn treatment using flaps and an artificial skin substitute called Biobrane. In Japan, artificial skin substitutes, including Biobrane, are generally not used in burn treatment, so I think I had a meaningful experience in that respect.

Next, in the Acute Medical Unit, where I did my clerkship, which is treated as a part of general medicine, they mainly see patients who come to the emergency department and need short-term inpatient care of two to three days. Naturally cardiovascular diseases are often handled. Here I was assigned relatively stable patients and was allowed to do the whole series of history taking, physical examination, assessment and presentation, and I learned a lot from it. What surprised me above all was that the local students' level in procedures in general, including physical examination, is high. Medical education at the University of Adelaide lasts six years, and from the first year practical examinations like the OSCE are imposed almost every year. At first, as in Japan, students only memorize the form of examination, but from the fourth year, when they begin clerkships, examinations with real patients are imposed. I was actually allowed to observe one, and they have to pass quite a difficult examination. The length of the course is the same as in Japan, but there is no equivalent of the national examination, and the examination imposed at the end of the fifth year is treated as effectively the national examination, while sixth-year students help residents and learn the real work. In other words, it is fair to think of a local sixth-year student as equivalent to a first-year resident in Japan. Under such circumstances, I was expected to perform at the same level as the local sixth-year students, so it was a quite tough clerkship, but I feel that what I gained was great.

In the Orthopedics and trauma unit, where I did my last clerkship, I mainly observed trauma treatment and operations for artificial joints such as THA and TKA. Cementless THA has recently been performed often in Japan and Europe, but at the Royal Adelaide Hospital, Professor Howie was a specialist in THA revision using a method called "cement within cement," so cement was also used even for primary THA. I put together slides combining what I had learned in clerkships at Nagoya University Hospital and other affiliated hospitals with knowledge I had researched in papers and so on, presented my thoughts on THA, and was able to have a discussion including feedback. This experience was very good, as it gave me the confidence that, if one has a solid knowledge background, one can have an advanced discussion even with some language barrier.

I was able to discover differences between medicine in Australia and in Japan, and differences in ways of thinking, in various respects, and I think that being made to think about them was a factor that greatly helped me grow during this study abroad. Japanese medicine is at a high standard even in the world, and I feel there is little medicine in the true sense that cannot be seen in Japan. If the purpose is training as a doctor, most treatment techniques can be learned within Japan. However, I think that the experience of going to a country with differences due to cultural background and values and seeing the medical front lines will, to no small degree, enlighten us Japanese. I intend to keep actively seeking opportunities to go overseas.

Lastly, I would like to close my account of my study abroad by expressing deep gratitude to the professors of the International Exchange Office, the people of the Academic Affairs Division, and the lecturers who took part in the pre-departure training, for their support in obtaining the valuable experience of this study abroad.
